title: No. 49 — Method of Guarding Against the Encroachments of Any One Department of Government by Appealing to the People Through a Convention. (Madison)
paragraphs: The author of the "Notes on the State of Virginia," quoted in the last paper, has appended to that valuable work the draft of a constitution. It had been prepared to be laid before a convention expected to be called in 1783 by the legislature, to establish a constitution for that commonwealth. The plan, like everything from the same pen, shows a turn of thinking that is original, comprehensive, and accurate. It deserves all the more attention because it equally displays a fervent attachment to republican government and an enlightened view of the dangerous tendencies against which it must be guarded. One of the precautions he proposes—on which he ultimately seems to rely as the safeguard of the weaker departments against invasions by the stronger—is perhaps entirely his own. Since it relates directly to our present inquiry, it should not be overlooked.

His proposal is, "that whenever any two of the three branches of government shall concur in opinion, each by the voices of two thirds of their whole number, that a convention is necessary for altering the constitution, or CORRECTING BREACHES OF IT, a convention shall be called for the purpose."

The people are the only legitimate fountain of power, and from them the constitutional charter—under which the several branches of government hold their power—is derived. So it seems strictly consistent with republican theory to return to that same original authority, not only whenever it may be necessary to enlarge, reduce, or remodel the powers of government, but also whenever any one of the departments encroaches on the chartered authorities of the others. The several departments are perfectly coordinate by the terms of their common commission. Clearly, none of them can claim an exclusive or superior right to settle the boundaries between their respective powers. So how are the encroachments of the stronger to be prevented, or the wrongs of the weaker to be redressed, without an appeal to the people themselves? As grantors of the commissions, only they can declare its true meaning and enforce its observance.

There is certainly great force in this reasoning. It must be allowed to prove that a constitutional road to the decision of the people should be marked out and kept open for certain great and extraordinary occasions. But there appear to be insurmountable objections against the proposed appeal to the people as a general provision for keeping the several departments within their constitutional limits.

First, the provision does not reach the case of a combination of two of the departments against the third. The legislative authority has many means of operating on the motives of the other departments. If it could win over either of the others—or even one third of its members—the remaining department could gain no advantage from this remedial provision. I do not dwell on this objection, because it might be thought to bear on the form of the principle rather than on the principle itself.

Second, there is an objection inherent in the principle. Every appeal to the people would imply some defect in the government. Frequent appeals would largely deprive the government of that veneration which time bestows on everything, and without which perhaps even the wisest and freest governments would not possess the necessary stability. If it is true that all governments rest on opinion, it is equally true that the strength of opinion in each individual, and its practical influence on his conduct, depend largely on how many he supposes share the same opinion. Human reason, like man himself, is timid and cautious when left alone. It gains firmness and confidence in proportion to the number with which it is associated. When the examples that fortify opinion are ANCIENT as well as NUMEROUS, they are known to have a double effect. In a nation of philosophers, this consideration could be ignored. Reverence for the laws would be sufficiently instilled by the voice of enlightened reason. But a nation of philosophers is as unlikely as the philosophical race of kings Plato wished for. In every other nation, the most rational government will not find it a superfluous advantage to have the prejudices of the community on its side.

An even more serious objection to frequent referrals of constitutional questions to the decision of the whole society is the danger of disturbing public tranquility by stirring up public passions too strongly. The revisions of our established forms of government have been successful, and that success does great honor to the virtue and intelligence of the American people. Even so, it must be admitted that the experiments are of too delicate a nature to be unnecessarily multiplied. We must remember that all the existing constitutions were formed in the midst of a danger which suppressed the passions most hostile to order and concord. They were formed amid an enthusiastic confidence of the people in their patriotic leaders, which silenced the ordinary diversity of opinion on great national questions. They were formed amid a universal ardor for new and opposite forms, produced by a universal resentment and indignation against the old government. And no spirit of party connected with the changes to be made, or the abuses to be reformed, could mix its leaven into the operation. The future situations in which we are usually likely to find ourselves do not offer any equivalent safeguard against the danger we anticipate.

But the greatest objection of all is this. The decisions that would probably result from such appeals would not serve the purpose of maintaining the constitutional balance of government. We have seen that the tendency of republican governments is toward an aggrandizement of the legislature at the expense of the other departments. So the appeals to the people would usually be made by the executive and judicial departments. But whether made by one side or the other, would each side enjoy equal advantages on trial? Consider their different situations. The members of the executive and judicial departments are few in number, and can be personally known to only a small part of the people. The judges, by the mode of their appointment as well as by its nature and permanence, are too far removed from the people to share much in their preferences. The executives are generally objects of jealousy, and their administration is always liable to be discolored and rendered unpopular. The members of the legislative department, by contrast, are numerous. They are distributed throughout and live among the people at large. Their connections of blood, friendship, and acquaintance embrace a large portion of the most influential part of society. The nature of their public trust implies a personal influence among the people, and that they are more directly the confidential guardians of the people's rights and liberties. With these advantages, it can hardly be supposed that the opposing party would have an equal chance of a favorable outcome.

But the legislative party would not only be able to plead their cause most successfully with the people. They would probably be constituted as the judges themselves. The same influence that had gained them election into the legislature would gain them a seat in the convention. If this should not be the case with all of them, it would probably be the case with many, and almost certainly with those leading figures on whom everything depends in such bodies. In short, the convention would be composed mainly of men who had been, were currently, or expected to be members of the department whose conduct was on trial. They would therefore be parties to the very question they were to decide.

Yet sometimes appeals might be made under circumstances less adverse to the executive and judicial departments. The usurpations of the legislature might be so flagrant and sudden as to admit no specious coloring. A strong party among the legislators themselves might side with the other branches. The executive power might be in the hands of a particular favorite of the people. In such a posture of things, the public decision might be less swayed by preferences for the legislative party. But still, it could never be expected to turn on the true merits of the question. It would inevitably be tied up with the spirit of pre-existing parties, or of parties springing out of the question itself. It would be tied up with persons of distinguished character and extensive influence in the community. It would be pronounced by the very men who had been agents in, or opponents of, the measures to which the decision related. The PASSIONS, therefore, not the REASON, of the public would sit in judgment. But it is the reason of the public, alone, that ought to control and regulate the government. The passions ought to be controlled and regulated by the government.

We found in the last paper that mere declarations in the written constitution are not sufficient to restrain the several departments within their legal rights. It appears in this paper that occasional appeals to the people would be neither a proper nor an effective provision for that purpose. How far the provisions of a different nature contained in the plan quoted above might be adequate, I do not examine. Some of them are unquestionably founded on sound political principles, and all are framed with remarkable ingenuity and precision.
